title: Underwater Sound by the Numbers
context: The four estimates are chosen as reusable sonar benchmarks: metre-scale wavelength at a kilohertz, multi-second propagation across tactical distances, hundreds of metres of depth per second of echo delay, and the inverse-square penalty from geometric spreading.
terms: Distance occupied by one cycle of a wave.
Elapsed time between emission and reception.
Depth measurement from two-way acoustic travel time.
Ideal dilution of energy across an expanding spherical area.

eqs.explain: Estimate 1,500 ÷ 1,000. A one-kilohertz tone therefore has a wavelength of about 1.5 metres—a useful reminder that low-frequency sonar wavelengths are physically large.
eqs.revealQ: What wavelength corresponds to the one-kilohertz training tone?
eqs.purpose: Memorable benchmark: in seawater, a one-kilohertz acoustic wave is roughly one and a half metres long.
eqs.prompt: How large is one wavelength of the training tone?

eqs.purpose: Memorable benchmark: underwater sound needs about ten seconds to travel fifteen kilometres.

factors.desc: A sphere's area scales with range squared, so ten times the range gives one hundred times the area.

eqs.explain: Ten times the range spreads the same idealized energy over one hundred times the area. The intensity therefore falls to one hundredth, or about one percent.
eqs.revealQ: What fraction of ideal intensity remains after the tenfold range increase?

sourceSummary: Every playable value is linked to an official source or an explicit conversion from a cited constant.
mission: Build four mental benchmarks for underwater acoustics. Choose the quantities that let an operator estimate wave scale, latency, depth, and ideal spreading without a calculator.
goals: Wave scale: connect a kilohertz tone with a metre-scale wavelength.
Latency: estimate how long sound needs to cross a tactical ocean distance.
Depth: turn a bottom-echo delay into an ocean-depth scale.
Spreading: recognize the intensity penalty from a tenfold increase in range.

title: Dead Reckoning and Current by the Numbers
context: The four estimates follow the core dead-reckoning questions a watch team repeatedly asks: how far the ship advanced, how far current set it sideways, how much heading correction the current requires, and how long remains to the waypoint.
terms: Advancing a known position using course, speed, and elapsed time.
The direction and speed with which current carries a vessel.
The vessel's actual rate of progress across the chart after current is included.

eqs.q: Bridge-watch advance: estimate the dead-reckoning distance.

factors.label: Steady ship speed
factors.desc: Defined representative underway speed.
factors.playDesc: Defined representative underway speed.

factors.label: Bridge-watch duration
factors.desc: Defined four-hour watch interval.
factors.playDesc: Defined four-hour watch interval.

eqs.explain: At twenty knots, the ship covers about twenty nautical miles each hour. Over a four-hour watch, advance the plot by roughly eighty nautical miles.
eqs.revealQ: How far should the dead-reckoning position advance during the bridge watch?
eqs.purpose: Memorable benchmark: a ship at twenty knots travels about eighty nautical miles in a four-hour watch.
eqs.prompt: How far should the plot advance during one bridge watch?

factors.playDesc: Defined interval between reliable position fixes.

eqs.explain: A two-and-a-half-knot cross-current moves the vessel about two and a half nautical miles sideways each hour. In two hours, the uncorrected set grows to about five nautical miles.
eqs.revealQ: How much cross-track error can accumulate before the next external fix?
eqs.purpose: Memorable benchmark: even a modest current can create several nautical miles of cross-track error between fixes.
eqs.prompt: How large can the cross-track error become before the next fix?

eqs.q: Current correction: estimate the small heading offset in degrees.

factors.label: Cross-current speed
factors.desc: Defined current perpendicular to the intended ground track.

eqs.explain: The current is about one tenth of ship speed, so the correction is about one tenth of a radian. One tenth of 57 degrees is roughly six degrees.
eqs.revealQ: About how many degrees into the current should the ship steer under the small-angle approximation?
eqs.purpose: Memorable benchmark: a cross-current near ten percent of ship speed requires roughly a six-degree correction.
eqs.prompt: About how far into the current should the ship steer?

eqs.revealQ: How much time remains before the ship reaches the waypoint?
eqs.purpose: Memorable benchmark: forty-five nautical miles at fifteen knots made good is a three-hour transit.
eqs.prompt: How much time remains to the waypoint?

sourceSummary: Scenario values are explicitly defined, and the unit conversion is linked to an institutional source.
mission: Maintain a navigation plot between external fixes. Build quick estimates for advance, lateral set, course correction, and arrival time using only the shared number bank.
goals: Advance: estimate how far a ship moves during a standard bridge watch.
Set: estimate the cross-track error accumulated before the next fix.
Correction: estimate the small angle needed to oppose a cross-current.
Arrival: estimate time to the next waypoint from speed made good.

title: Pressure and Buoyancy at Depth
context: The estimates are designed around four reusable hydrostatic benchmarks: roughly one megapascal per hundred metres, pressure multiplied by area gives very large hatch loads, each cubic metre of seawater supplies about ten kilonewtons of buoyancy, and each flooded cubic metre adds roughly one tonne of mass.
terms: Pressure created by the weight of a fluid column.
Pressure measured relative to the surrounding atmosphere.
Volume of water displaced by a submerged or floating body.
Upward force equal to the weight of displaced fluid in the ideal static case.

eqs.purpose: Memorable benchmark: one hundred metres of seawater adds roughly one megapascal, about ten atmospheres, of gauge pressure.

title: Radar Horizon and Timing by the Numbers
context: The four estimates build an operational radar scale: a low shipboard horizon, electromagnetic travel measured in microseconds, pulse width translated into range resolution, and detection range translated into minutes of reaction time.
terms: The line-of-sight limit imposed primarily by Earth curvature for low targets.
Elapsed time between transmission and echo reception.
The minimum range separation at which two targets can be distinguished by pulse timing.
Time between detection and arrival at the defended position under the simplified geometry.

factors.unit: nautical miles per square root metre

source.label: Defined conversion from NASA horizon relation

factors.playDesc: Derived from Earth-curvature geometry and unit conversion, neglecting refraction.

factors.label: Square root of antenna height
factors.desc: Square root of the defined twenty-five-metre antenna height.
factors.playDesc: Square root of the defined twenty-five-metre antenna height.

eqs.explain: The square root of twenty-five metres is five. Multiplying by roughly two nautical miles per square-root metre gives a horizon near ten nautical miles.
eqs.revealQ: How far away is the shipboard radar's geometric horizon?
eqs.purpose: Memorable benchmark: a radar about twenty-five metres above the sea has a geometric horizon of roughly ten nautical miles.
eqs.prompt: How far away is the radar's direct line-of-sight horizon?
